item.research_question: What are the elastic and plastic deformation behaviors of the NbTaTiV refractory high-entropy alloy at room temperature and elevated temperatures, and how do they compare to conventional BCC alloys?
item.material_system: Nb23.8Ta25.5Ti24.9V25.8 (nominally Nb25Ta25Ti25V25) BCC refractory high-entropy alloy
item.processing_route: Arc melting under argon atmosphere from 99.99 wt% purity elements, melted 10 times, drop-cast into 4-mm diameter rods, homogenized at 1200°C for 3 days, followed by water cooling
item.test_conditions: In situ neutron diffraction and compressive testing at room temperature (RT), 500°C, 700°C, and 900°C with a strain rate of 1 × 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹; Resonant Ultrasound Spectroscopy (RUS) at RT; First-principles calculations at -273°C and RT
key_findings: The alloy exhibits a single BCC solid solution phase stable up to 900°C with grain sizes of 200 to 400 μm.
Yield strength decreases from 1064 MPa at RT to 595 MPa at 900°C.
The alloy shows elastically isotropic deformation behavior at RT, with a Zener anisotropy ratio (A_Z) of approximately 1.2 and a universal anisotropy index (A_U) of 0.
Elastic anisotropy gradually increases at elevated temperatures, but the variation is much smaller than in conventional alloys (A_Z increases from 1.2 at RT to 1.6 at 900°C).
The dominant mobile dislocations during plastic deformation are <111>{110} edge dislocations, unlike conventional BCC metals where screw dislocations often dominate.
The alloy is intrinsically ductile, indicated by a Pugh ratio (K/G) > 1.75 and Poisson's ratio (ν) > 0.26 across all tested temperatures.
The Kroner model provides the best agreement with experimental diffraction elastic moduli, with absolute percentage standard errors of 2.46% at RT and 8.85% at 900°C.
Machine learning models predicted shear and bulk moduli with relative errors of 2.5% and 6%, respectively, despite being trained on ordered compounds.
item.mechanism: The authors argue that the severe lattice distortion caused by the random distribution of multiple elements with different atomic radii leads to the deviation of edge dislocation cores from their neutral planes, creating wavy dislocation lines. This feature, induced by compositional fluctuations, reduces the mobility of edge dislocations, making them the dominant mobile dislocation type, which contrasts with conventional BCC metals. The elastic isotropy at RT is attributed to the specific valence electron concentration (VEC ≈ 4.68) and the resulting balance of elastic constants.
item.limitations: The authors note that the validity of theoretical calculation methods for designing elastically isotropic and ductile BCC HEAs was previously lacking experimental validation, which this study addresses but implies further work is needed. They also mention that the ML model's good agreement is somewhat unexpected given the training data only contained ordered compounds, and the lattice distortion effect in HEAs might cause less accurate results, though lack of data prevents full assessment.
item.future_work: The authors propose that these discoveries will facilitate the development of possible alloy systems for structural material applications and provide a road map toward the discovery and production of newly designed polycrystalline materials.
quotes: The present work discovers the unique deformation behavior of a refractory high-entropy alloy at elevated temperatures.
It is found that the dominant type of mobile dislocations during plastic deformation could be edge dislocations, which is different from conventional BCC metals.
The NbTaTiV BCC refractory HEA exhibits no orientation-dependent lattice strain evolutions during elastic deformation at RT, leading to nearly similar values of elastic moduli in differently grains.

item.research_question: How to determine the elastic constants and derived moduli of a NbTaTiV refractory high-entropy alloy using Resonant Ultrasound Spectroscopy (RUS) across a specific frequency range.
item.test_conditions: Cylindrical sample corner-mounted between two transducers; frequency swept through the 100- to 650-kHz range; elastic isotropy assumed.
key_findings: Elastic constants C11, C12, and C44 were determined using sample dimensions and observed resonances.
Large responses were detected when the frequency corresponded to an eigenfrequency of the sample.
Bulk modulus (K) and shear modulus (G) were determined using Hill's approximations.
item.mechanism: The authors assume elastic isotropy and derive elastic constants from the sample's resonant frequencies and dimensions, then calculate bulk and shear moduli via Hill's approximations.
quotes: Assuming that the elastic isotropy and the elastic constants, ( C 11 , C 12 , and C 44 ), were determined, using sample dimensions, and observed resonances.
In our study, the frequency was swept through the 100- to 650-kHz range with large responses detected when the frequency corresponds to an eigenfrequency of the sample.
From the elastic constants, bulk modulus ( K ) and shear modulus ( G ) were determined using Hill's approximations ( [40] ).
